subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would the
Prime Minister be willing to tell the house the circumstances under which the Minister of Transport had an audience with the Queen? Was that at the request of the Canadian government, and had it to do with the flag question?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister was in England on a private visit and, as is quite normal for ministers of the crown, he asked for an audience with the Queen and was granted an audience. He informed Her Majesty of the terms personally, as she had been informed by cable, of the resolution which will be before the house shortly.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Did the Prime Minister tell the premier of Newfoundland that the Minister of Transport was going to London in order to consult with the Queen on this question?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Then, Mr. Speaker, so there will be no mistake about it, I would like to ask the Prime Minister to table the correspondence between himself and Premier Smallwood, and in particular the wire dated May 27 in which Mr. Smallwood received information on this question. I would like to direct the Prime Minister's attention to Premier Smallwood's words. The following is a report appearing in the Evening Telegram of May 29:
Premier J. R. Smallwood told an A.Y.P.A. gathering in St. John's last night-
That was May 28:
-that the Newfoundland representative in the federal cabinet, transport minister J. W. Pickersgill, was in London Thursday night to see Her Majesty the Queen on the flag issue.
The premier said he was informed of this by Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport did not go over to London to see the Queen on this or any other matter. He
was in London and asked for an audience with the Queen to inform the Queen of the terms of the resolution, as I have just said, which was on the order paper and of which she had been informed by telegram. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that is a normal and courteous procedure to adopt.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: That is not an answer to my question, which was whether the Prime Minister told Mr. Smallwood, when he had not told parliament, that the Minister of Transport went over there for the purpose of discussing with the Queen the question of the flag.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I have just said that he did not go over for that purpose.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Did the Prime Minister tell Mr. Smallwood that? The answer is silence.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Yes or no.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I asked a question yesterday-

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I should like to put a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: A supplementary question-

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Order. I have recognized the hon. member for Lapointe.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: This is a supplementary question in reference to one I asked yesterday.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the Prime Minister tell us whether the union jack constitutes the royal standard of England, Canada, Australia and other countries of the commonwealth or whether the Queen has her own standard and colours?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the union jack is the royal union standard. The Queen also, has a personal standard.

Inquiries of the Ministry [Translation]

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the Prime Minister tell us what other countries of the commonwealth of British nations have provided in their statutes that the union jack could be flown as a symbol of their adherence to the commonwealth of British nations?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I will have to make inquiries about that, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: You certainly will.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and is asked in view of his answer to the Leader of the Opposition. Did he have that knowledge yesterday when he answered me and said he did not know why the Minister of Transport went to Great Britain and why he had an audience with the Queen?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I do not yet know why the Minister of Transport went on a private visit to Great Britain.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Hon. gentlemen may laugh, but the Minister of Transport informed me a week or ten days ago that he would be in Great Britain on private business if that were agreeable to me, and for the days involved I agreed. I suggested that when the Minister of Transport was in England if he wished to have an audience with the Queen on this matter it would be quite proper to do so, and I do not apologize for that at all.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he will take into consideration the statement made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, according to a report published in the June 1 issue of the Sherbrooke La Tribune, said the following:
I do not like the idea of two flags.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I will be glad to take that statement into account, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question. In view of the answers he has just given, could he tell us if the Minister of Transport was sent to London to meet Her Majesty after some kind of consultation had taken place between the Prime Minister of Canada and the premier of Newfoundland, because apparently, during his stay in London the Minister of Transport

wishes to obtain the Queen's approval, and this seems to agree so much with what Premier Smallwood will impose or try to impose on the Canadian government?
Did the Prime Minister of Canada have talks with the premier of Newfoundland in anticipation of a consultation between the Minister of Transport and Her Majesty the Queen?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Order, please. I had hoped that I would not have to refer to this matter again, but I cannot restrict the hon. member for Kootenay West and then allow other hon. members to ask far too long questions. The question which has just been asked, if I may again refer to the reasons I gave yesterday, would seem to conflict with at least three of the new rules; namely, that the question is far too long; that it contains observations which might lead to debate; and it refers to a debate or to answers given to questions during the current session. If I worked diligently I suppose I could find a few other reasons. May I call to the attention of hon. members the fact that we have had a long series of questions. The opportunity to debate this important matter will be given before too long, I suspect, and I would counsel hon. members to phrase their questions in as short a manner as possible and directly to the point.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, I shall make my question much shorter. Did the Prime Minister of Canada send the Minister of Transport to London after having consulted with the premier of Newfoundland, to achieve the results we have now?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: The premier of Newfoundland had nothing to do with the arrangements regarding the audience of the Minister of Transport with the Queen, nor did he make any effort to have anything to do with them.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: As a further supplementary question, if the Minister of Transport went on private matters would the Prime Minister now disclose to the house whether he went over at government expense or at his own expense?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: I cannot answer that. However, I shall be glad to find the answer. The hon. member is asking me questions of detail which he knows cannot be answered at this time, but I will be very glad to find out the answers.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want the words of this question to the Prime Minister

to come strictly within the rules, as 1 thought they had earlier. I ask the Prime Minister, in view of Premier Smallwood's statement regarding this matter, also in view of the fact that he said it was an honour that a Newfoundland minister had been chosen for this mission to the Queen, will he table the telegrams that passed between him and Premier Smallwood, his reply being dated May 27, at 10.22 p.m.? Can we also have the telegram from Mr. Smallwood so that we can resolve this apparent dispute or uncertainty as between the views of the Prime Minister and the premier of Newfoundland?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be glad to ask Premier Smallwood for permission to table his telegram, and I would certainly be very glad to table my own.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister and ask him can he tell us whether the
Minister of Transport made this trip on a commercial flight or whether he used one of the government's planes.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: The Minister of Transport will be in the house tomorrow and he will be able to answer this.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: A man on a mission.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Can he tell us whether, before the passage of the resolution respecting the Canadian flags, we will have to rescind the order in council of 1945 respecting the red ensign?

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: We will be able to deal with these questions when the resolution is debated. On the point just raised by the Minister of Labour and others in regard to the method-

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext: This just shows my continuing regard for the hon. gentleman. In regard to the curiosity displayed as to whether the Minister of Transport paid his own fare, I have just been informed that the Minister of Transport went to England by T.C.A. commercial flight, accompanied by his wife and daughter. He will be returning alone today. He bought his own tickets and the visit had been arranged some time ago, long before the question of the Queen's audience arose. I hope my hon. friends' curiosity into the affairs of the Minister of Transport is now satisfied.

subtopic: AUDIENCE WITH HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN BY TRANSPORT MINISTER
speechtext:

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could divert the government's attention to something a bit more important, and ask the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources whether his attention has been drawn to the fact that the Skeena river is at least approaching the levels of the 1948 flood; that it is flooding in the Bird's lake area; that some bridges are in danger of being washed out by potential floods, not only there but in other parts of B.C.; and may I ask the minister if he would use his good offices to work in conjunction with the provincial government to prevent any disaster occurring in that entire area.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER
speechtext: Order, please. Yesterday we had a question on the Fraser river and it was allowed because it was very urgent and I understood the flood conditions could be quite serious. This question does not seem to have the same urgency. Would the hon. member put it on the order paper?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER
speechtext: It has precisely the same urgency, because the lives and property of people are involved in the flooding of the Skeena river just as dangerously as in the flooding of the Fraser river in 1948.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER
speechtext: Would the hon. member put it on the order paper; and may I quote the rules of the house which have been furnished to me, and of which the hon. member must know?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-POTENTIAL DANGERS ON SKEENA RIVER

maintopic: STEPS TO IMPROVE REPORTED LOW PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Last week eggs sold in Napanee for 21 cents a dozen. What is the minister doing to improve the ridiculously low price for this product now being produced at far below cost by the poultrymen of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: STEPS TO IMPROVE REPORTED LOW PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have a stabilization board, with which I am sure the hon. member must be very familiar, which supports eggs at 34 cents a dozen. the second reading of Bill No. S-21, to authorize the construction and maintenance of a bridge across the St. Lawrence river between the city of Ste. Foy, in the county of Quebec and the municipality of St. Nicolas, in the county of Levis, both in the province of Quebec.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill authorizing the construction and maintenance of a bridge over the St. Lawrence river, between the town of Ste. Foy, in the county of Quebec, and the municipality of St. Nicolas, in the county of Levis.
This bridge will be situated very near to the present Quebec bridge, perhaps a thousand feet up the river from the present bridge. The purpose of this bill is to comply with the Navigable Waters Act, which requires an act passed by parliament. If hon. members will pass this bill, I can assure them that the work will not begin until the plans and specifications have been examined by the experts of the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport. If, after examination of those plans and specifications, no impediment to navigation is found, an order in council will be passed so as to permit the province of Quebec to proceed with building the bridge.
The same procedure was followed, a few months ago, with regard to the Boucherville bridge, and I do not think it necessary to add any further detail at this stage, because this is just an authorization. It will not cost the Canadian government a single cent, for either the construction or the maintenance of that bridge. This is simply to give an authorization, and if hon. members want further information about this matter, I shall be happy to give it to them when we reach the committee stage.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF CONSTRUCTION BETWEEN STE. FOY AND ST. NICOLAS, QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad, on behalf of the official opposition, to give my support to the proposal just put before the house by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets).
Under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, all works carried out on or above the St. Lawrence river must be approved either by the Department of Public Works or the Department of Transport. Such approval takes the form of an order in council passed by the Canadian government.
As pointed out by the Minister of Public Works, the bridge will be parallel to the present Quebec bridge. The tremendous increase in traffic in that area has made it absolutely necessary to build this new bridge, and I believe it will be of very great service to the people.
Of course, that decision rests with the provincial government and I am not in a position to discuss the amounts that will be spent by the provincial government for those various undertakings.
However, I hope that the Minister of Public Works, when the various clauses of the bill are under consideration, will be able to give
Ste. Foy-St. Nicolas Bridge us information of interest to the federal authorities because, in short, the responsibility of the federal government is to make sure that nothing will interfere with navigation or ice movements.
Moreover, I understand that it is a suspension bridge. In my opinion, it is most important to know if piers will be built in the St. Lawrence river, and if they will be located in the channel of the river. Moreover, it must be known also if those piers could eventually delay the normal flow of ice or create ice-jams. As a matter of fact, the minister might tell us if the construction of that bridge will entail the services of an icebreaker during the winter months.
We know that at the present time there is an icebreaker in service in Quebec harbour. The job of that icebreaker is to make sure that there are no jams around the piers of the Quebec bridge so that the bridge is not affected by the ice. I hope the minister will be in a position to give us that information a little later.
Mr. Speaker, there is another matter which I do not wish to labour very long, but in which I am greatly interested. I refer to a bridge spanning the St. Lawrence river and built by the provincial government.
Just recently, I had the opportunity to be present at the formal beginning of the construction of the Three Rivers bridge, a most important bridge, since it links the most important city in Canada to the south shore.

Mr. Speaker, it was only to be expected that the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) would congratulate the government which will do for the Quebec area what it has done lately for the Three Rivers area..

Ste. Foy-St. Nicolas Bridge
However, in spite of the fact that this problem does not come under our jurisdiction, since part of the bridge will be situated in the Quebec-Montmorency constituency- in the bill, Quebec is probably mentioned because it refers to a provincial constituency, but the federal riding is Quebec-Montmorency -and since especially the mayor of Levis mentioned some time ago and has repeated quite often since that the project is absolutely fantastic and ridiculous, I wonder whether we should not try to stop it.
However, that is none of our business, and it will be up to the people of the province of Quebec to judge the actions of the provincial government.
That bridge is located only a few hundred feet from the present Quebec bridge. The purpose of building that bridge is to alleviate traffic, but its approaches will be those now used for the Quebec bridge. Mr. Speaker, I wonder really what the provincial authorities were thinking about when they decided on building that bridge which, no doubt, will afford better facilities to cross the river, but people will not be able to use it because traffic before reaching the bridge will be too heavy during rush hours.
A few years ago the Quebec board of trade as well as other organizations prepared a brief in which it stated that the best way to alleviate traffic to and from Quebec would not be to improve the situation on and around the Quebec bridge, nor to build a tunnel between Levis and Quebec city; it would be better to build a bridge more to the east, that is between the island of Orleans and the municipality of Beaumont which is located on the other side of the river. That would make it possible to solve the traffic problem for the people coming from the lower St. Lawrence region who want to cross at Quebec city to go to Chicoutimi, the Saguenay area or the north shore. That would also enable the people coming from the Saguenay area or the north shore who want to go to Gaspe or the south shore, to get there directly, without having to go right through Quebec city to its western limits in order to take a bridge that will not be more efficient than the first because of its access roads.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want to stop this bill because the federal government has simply to make sure that the new bridge will not interfere with navigation in any way, win meet all the requirements of the Department of Transport and will not interfere either with the free flow of ice in winter.
If all those conditions are met, of course we will accept it. But since a part of this bridge wfll be in my riding-and even if it had been logically placed between Orleans

island and Beaumont on the south shore, it would also have been in my riding-and as I am very much interested in this question, I want to point out, that in my opinion, the purpose which was stated by the provincial authorities is quite wrong. And I know, from a very reliable source, that some people bought land in the neighbourhood of the proposed bridge and that they will be in a position to sell those lots for the construction of the bridge, a thing which they would not be able to do if it were built on the east side of Quebec city.
I shall quote, once more, the statements of the mayor of Levis, to the effect that it is absurd to build a bridge near the other one, because they would be too close, and also because the second one would lead to a municipality much less important, St. Romuald- I understand that, like for the city of Three Rivers, it is for its inhabitants the greatest city in the world, but on the south shore, the economic complex actually surrounds the city of Levis. Besides, that is the opinion of the mayor of Levis who feels he is managing one of the largest cities on the south shore. However, as far as I am concerned, I would go much farther to the east, that is between Orleans island and Beaumont. The bridge would then achieve the specific purpose for which it is being built.
Once again, I want to call your attention to the fact that individuals may have bought land near the site of the proposed bridge in order to take advantage of the sale of those lots. Indeed, can any level-headed person imagine the reasons for the construction of a bridge about 1,400 feet west of the first one. If any one can think of a good reason, I would be glad to hear it, and to admit that this project is sensible.

I cannot believe that there is any patronage in Quebec any more, not with the government of Jean Lesage. That is one of the reasons I feel it is most unfortunate that the hon. member raised this, because in a way it is irrelevant to the bill but it does cast a bit of a slur on this great government of Jean Lesage, incorruptible and set off on a new course in Quebec provincial politics.
The hon. member for Lapointe tells me Lili St. Cyr is no longer there but that there still is patronage. Actually Lili St. Cyr was a foreign element, and I am sure patronage is also a foreign element under the great government of Jean Lesage. The predictions concerning this bill are that federal jurisdiction and federal responsibility will not come under any particular difficulty or strain, always remembering of course that so far as the Three Rivers bridge was concerned, depending which argument you supported, the federal government might have responsibility for up to $60 million as a result of something that had been entered into by the federal Department of Transport.
We are going to support this bill, Mr. Speaker, but we confess that we do not know a great deal about the implications that are involved, as referred to by the hon. member in whose riding it is going to be built. These definitely raise certain doubts in our minds which I hope the minister can allay. If, as the mayor of Levis has said, this is a ridiculous and silly kind of business, the minister should let us have his reactions to this. He should tell us whether he is approaching it simply from the point of view that the province is within its rights to ask for this, and ours is not to ask the reason why but to do or die. I take it that is his attitude. If he gives us the assurance that the insurance provisions of the bill are adequate, we are prepared to support it.
It seems to me there is really not much more one can say in this kind of thing except to make certain that the engineers of the federal government have looked at the situation and have ascertained that the provincial government cannot get involved in some kind of projection that will cause navigation difficulties. I suppose that in regard to anything connected with the Quebec bridge everyone always remembers the history of the structure, the disaster that took place there many years ago, and the fact that it was one of the great political incidents in our parliamentary history. Because there is no question in this particular case of a federal contribution I

We had an identical situation on the island of Montreal when the previous government, and I commend them for it, built the magnificent Champlain bridge, which is situated only a few thousand yards upstream from the Victoria bridge and downstream from the Mercier bridge. I think the construction of the Champlain bridge has contributed greatly to the development of the south shore, and I humbly suggest to the members of this house that the construction of a new bridge in the general area of the present Quebec bridge will have at least as one of its side effects the hastening of the development of the south shore of the Quebec city area.

I agree, of course, with my hon. friend for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) that the problem of communication does exist in his particular part of Quebec. There again bridges are needed, and I think it is the general conclusion of those who are familiar with Quebec city and its problems of communication and development that the area needs to be serviced by more bridges or possibly more tunnels. I think the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), whom I respect, touched on a very significant point when he emphasized that one of Quebec city's greatest attractions is its characteristic beauty, and of necessity this must be shown and made as convenient as possible for tourists to reach. The tourist trade as it is developing at the moment flows into Quebec city usually from New York state and from Montreal, and first contact with the city of Quebec is generally made in the vicinity of the present Quebec bridge. So from that aspect if no other I think it is high time that a new bridge is built in that area.
I also agree, as a student in and friend of Quebec city, that the time is coming when construction of other means of communication between Quebec and Levis, Montmorency and through to the island of Orleans must be provided. I think that this bridge is the first step only in the eventual development of communications on the island. In this regard I congratulate the members from Quebec who are normally so very jealous in this house of provincial rights and jurisdiction and who feel it is almost a sin to criticize the province of Quebec. I am glad to see so many Quebec members assuming their rights as federal members of parliament and passing judgment on what is happening in the province of Quebec. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. S-18, respecting the Montreal board of trade.

subtopic: MONTREAL BOARD OF TRADE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: MONTREAL BOARD OF TRADE
speechtext:
Bill No. S-18, an act respecting the Montreal board of trade, is in essence similar to hundreds of other such bills which have come before this house in previous sessions.
I would beg the indulgence of hon. members for a few moments to draw to their attention that at a time in our history when we are more than ever aware of our heritage the Montreal board of trade is requesting a minor adjustment in its charter to assist the development of an organization which was formed not 50, or 100 years ago, but in 1822, 142 years ago. It is significant, I think, that human nature rarely changes. Back in 1822, a group of merchants, dissatisfied with the chaotic conditions of the time, banded together to improve the trade and commerce of the island of Montreal by some form of organization. Trade at that time was impeded by laborious methods of communication which necessitated decisions being made and bills being regulated in England; it often took three months before decisions could be rendered. Twenty years later, in 1842, these merchants were granted a royal charter which gave them certain powers on the island of Montreal. I do not intend to discuss these powers in detail, but they have some history attached to them. For instance, members of the board of trade were given the task of policing weights and measures and controlling the quality of flour, meat and so forth. They grew in reputation and respect and were eventually granted exemption from jury service, in those days a mark of esteem granted only after careful deliberation. I think, however, that the Montreal board of trade will best be recognized, at least by members from my area, for the fact that it was directly concerned with the establishment of the great port of Montreal and directly responsible for the system of canals which permitted trade to flow up the great lakes into what is now Canada.
In those days the board of trade took an active part not only in the expansion of trade and commerce but in the field of education both of its own members and of the citizens of the island generally. Since then, of course, the work of the board has changed considerably. Many of the functions that were performed at that time have been taken over
Private Bills
by municipal, provincial and federal organizations. However, the board of trade is still of tremendous usefulness in the business world of Montreal and it maintains direct relationship with trade matters. For instance, it has developed one of the most complete libraries in the world on the subject of exportation and importation, and today it renders a most useful service to its members by providing information on tariffs and so forth. The Montreal board of trade has continued to serve the community for 142 consecutive years and today it is as vigorous as it ever was. Some 2,800 firms in the Montreal area, both large and small, are among its members.
Unfortunately its present premises in the historic centre of Montreal, on St. Sacrament street, were built between 1900 and 1903 and are no longer adequate. Moreover, the efficiency of the board is lessened by the fact that the geographical face of Montreal has changed. Today, St. Sacrament street is no longer the hub of the world of enterprise in the city. Business has a tendency now to move uptown, as it is commonly called. In order that the board may become more efficient and serve its members better, it is desired to move to what is commonly known as uptown. Such a move is presently being held up, and one of the reasons is the fact that in 1890 a minor change in the board's charter limited the real holdings of the board to $1 million. Certainly, in 1890, $1 million was a considerable sum of money and it stood the board in good stead until the present day. As all members who are familiar with the city of Montreal know, the cost of buying land and erecting a building on a suitable location is such that this limitation to $1 million is proving an impediment; it is holding the board back. A similar problem affecting the Toronto board of trade was, I believe, placed before this house some time ago.
In these circumstances, the board is seeking to end the limitation imposed upon it in 1890. It is asking that the restriction to physical holdings of $1 million be removed so that it may feel free to move to a new location and thus continue its fine work for the business community of Montreal. I would humbly ask that this request be acceded to, and if the bill should pass second reading today that it be referred to the standing committed on banking and commerce where witnesses may be called for or against the proposal.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on banking and commerce.

He said: I invite the attention of the house with my usual brevity, of course, to a bill the passage of which would I believe do something to strengthen our sense of national purpose and mark at least one step away from those long years of Canadian neglect of the great men whose labours and vision have made our land great.
One is appalled to note how little is known about Sir John A. Macdonald. The minister of education in the great province of Ontario was alarmed when he discovered that many school children, otherwise well informed, knew not the name of the father of our country. And I have noted on a certain radio program emanating from Ottawa where they question listeners about the names of various characters-and they do not always get them right-there is no alacrity of response when they inquire about Sir John A. Macdonald. Indeed, in Canada, while thousands would know the birth date of Abraham Lincoln or George Washington it would require a little research to find the birth date of Sir John A. Macdonald. We recognize St. Patrick's day and St. Andrew's day, as is right and proper. We recognize Robert Burns day, too. But I am inviting the house to set apart a Sir John A. Macdonald day. In doing so, no party here represented would suffer and I think all would gain something by recognizing what the great Joseph Howe said long ago-I shall quote his words, as many hon. members have done before me.
A wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its muniments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures and fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
My hon. friend from Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Alkenbrack) did a real service when in connection with an earlier bill brought before this house he dealt with the career of our great first, first minister who was born on January 11, 1815. They know what manner of man he was-the great John A., the lovable John A., the puckish John A.; although at times he was plunged into the loneliness of despair and the unhappiness of frustration, beset by doubts and anxiety-and, heaven knows, he has reason enough for both. And he was not a teetotaler; I think that is

now part of the record. He was quite a hard drinker. Indeed, he said in those memorable words:
The people of Canada would rather have John A. drunk than George Brown sober.
He demonstrated the accuracy of his prophecy, if not the virtue of his habits. He was a man who, entering public life in 1844, remained in public life for nearly half a century; a cabinet minister for a third of a century, and prime minister for nearly 20 years. A gay man was John A.; a popular man; a beloved man, but also a great man. What were the secrets of his greatness and what in his life, in his record, is of value to us today? I think much. First he was a nation builder; a practical man of common sense and shrewd judgment. In one of his first speeches in the old legislature of Canada he stood up and said:
In a young country like Canada I am of the opinion that it is of more consequence to endeavour to develop its resources and improve its physical advantages than to waste the time of the legislature and the money of the people in fruitless discussions on abstract and theoretical questions of government.
We do not have many political philosophers in Canada, and we Conservatives can claim that John A. Macdonald was one of them. Yet with all his hardbitten common sense he was a visionary. He saw a greater Canada. When others saw only narrow, small confines for the little political communities of what was then British North America in the middle of the 19th century, he saw a transcontinental dominion and he made his vision a reality. Of him Laurier said:
His actions displayed a far reaching vision beyond the event of the day, and, still higher, permeating the whole, a broad patriotism, a devotion to Canada's welfare, Canada's advancement and Canada's glory. It may be said without any exaggeration whatsoever that the life of Sir John A. Macdonald, from the day he entered parliament, is the history of Canada.
That is what the great Laurier said about the great Macdonald. It was not easy for him to pursue his vision of a transcontinental dominion. We think at times in our political life today that we have bitterness, but the days in which Sir John A. functioned were replete with invective and political suspicion of motives which were not always quite above reproach. The suggestions involved in his new state were so difficult, but resisting alike the blandishments of those who would surrender supinely to incorporate them with the great republican neighbour and those whose range could not transcend a weak, inglorious colonialism, he and his associates built a country monarchical and free, American yet not republican, dedicated to the British institution from which it sprang but destined

surely for independence, with its own unique political institutions, the greatest of which is that in which we are all functionaries. It is well known that in his last great campaign, when he faced what he thought was a great danger to Canada's continuing independence he made this stirring statement. He was not the greatest orator of his time, but he said:
Shall we endanger our possession of the great heritage bequeathed to us by our fathers, and submit ourselves to direct taxation for the privilege of having our tariff fixed at Washington, with the prospect of ultimately becoming a portion of the American union?...As for myself, my course is clear. A British subject X was born-a British subject I will die. With my utmost effort, with my latest breath, will I oppose the "veiled treason" which attempts by sordid means and mercenary proffers to lure our people from their allegiance.
It was almost his "latest breath", because the election of 1891 killed Sir John A. Macdonald. But he was something else, and I think this is of interest to all of us. He was a party man. Macdonald always said his greatest work was done before confederation. Some historians would question that. But he did see, like Bryce and many other students of politics saw later, that political parties are actually older than democracy and that no great free country can exist long without them. In 1854, with great finesse, with infinite patience, with broadmindedness, with understanding, with good fellowship, with a sense of purpose, he joined the Progressive Conservative party, then called the Liberal Conservative party. Then in 1864, the year of the Charlottetown conference, through the great magnanimity of a man who was not always magnanimous, George Brown, he formed a coalition and so came to Charlottetown with a united political group in 1864. There again the gifts and abilities of the man when he built a party were applied to creating a nation; and we know what emanated from that great meeting in the city which I have the honour to represent in this House of Commons.
The architect of confederation was also the father of Canada's great historic parties. He did in his time what Sir Wilfrid Laurier was to do a few years later. He created, inspired and led the second great national party, and when we reached that stage we reached a mature political society, broadly based, with a unified course. In any country such as ours where regional feelings and backgrounds are strong, differences are never too far below the surface, differences of religion, ethnic background, economic inequality, geographic separation. In spite of all these discordant forces Canada, first under the great Liberal Conservative party and then-and I cannot pretend that it is quite as good as the one I have just
Private Bills
mentioned-under the Liberal party of Laurier, was brought together with a great degree of unity and there was progress in this country.
He was something else than a party man. He was a moderate. In an age when it was so easy to ring the welkin on particularism, on regionalism, and indeed on bigotry, he took another course. Macdonald, in his close association with Cartier was surely an essential factor in confederation and the building of the party which became the vehicle ushering in confederation. In a day of bigotry and bitterness he avoided both. As a great Canadian historian-I think not a Conservative one; I was a student of this man-Professor Lower, has said:
His stand with respect to the race question was consistent throughout his life whatever the cost to himself...he refused to raise the race cry at a time when he was in low political water.
His words to Brown Chamberlain, editor of the Montreal Gazette, further clarify his attitude:
The trouble is that you British Canadians can never forget that you were once supreme, that John Baptiste was once your hewer of wood and drawer of water. You struggle for ascendancy. If a Lower Canadian Britisher-
That is quite an expression, Mr. Speaker, but it was recognized in those days:
-desires to conquer he must stoop to conquer. He must make friends with the French without sacrificing the principles of his race or lineage. He must respect their nationality. Treat them as a nation; and they will act as a free people generally do-generously. Treat them as a faction and they will become factious.
So he wrote many years ago. As the professor says:
Wise words-the beginning and the end of our Canadian puzzle but by few indeed taken to heart. Can the man who wrote them and who lived them be accused of having been a "mere opportunist".
Then at another time when his own party was torn because of excessive religious particularism, if I may use the euphemism, although it is more than that; when the country was being torn apart by one of the greatest of all political ills, and the identification of an ethnic region and a geographic region within a political party line became threatening he said:
Let us forget this cry and we shall have our reward in seeing this unfortunate fire which has been kindled from so small a spark extinguished forever and we shall go on as we have been going on since 1867 as one people with one object, looking to one future and expecting to lay the foundations of one great country.
Macdonald was always a one-Canada man; he was always a strong-Canada man; and he did not hesitate to use the greatness of the national political apparatus to further national aims and to strengthen national purpose.

Private Bills
There is much one would like to say about this man whom we should honour more, but I can only conclude my remarks, so inadequate to the greatness of my subject, by calling on the members of this house. We are at this moment in danger of embarking upon another sea of discord. Let us find out whether out of our historic past and our common tradition there is something to symbolize greater unity, something around which we as Canadians and we members of this house as legislators may find a rallying point.
We Canadians are perhaps not very picturesque people. We are not terribly emotional. We are a bit casual about many things and certainly about our history. I would invite the support of this bill to honour the founder of our country, which sets aside a day when we, like him, can move our thoughts in the direction of unity and of greatness, away from discord and those matters which would separate us and undo those things which would bind us together. Because only thus can that land which he and his associates built up and is called Canada be worthy of his name.

maintopic: SIR JOHN A. MACDONALD PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF LEGAL HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to follow and to support the urbane, erudite and always affable member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), whose presence in this house has ever provided an aura of grace and decorum in an often times tempestuous place. I would point out that the hon. member, in presenting to the house a bill whereby we might pay some homage and honour to the attorney general for Canada west, as he was prior to confederation, is doing something which many of us in this house feel is important. He is doing something which should have been done before and something to which we should all give our very serious and considered attention. I would certainly agree with the hon. member when he states that too often in the past in this country, and in this house in particular, we have ill honoured our past. We have not paid sufficient homage to our history, and in so doing we have probably failed to strengthen that foundation for this nation which can only be made strong, and on which we can build a greater future, if we honour and strengthen our past as the hon. member would have us do.
With respect to Sir John A. Macdonald, whom the hon. member would have us honour here, I would point out that certainly some considerable tribute has been paid to him in the biography of Donald Creighton, who I understand to be of a similar political vintage both of the hon. member and to Sir John A. Macdonald, as a result of which his 
two-volume biography may have been somewhat coloured but is nevertheless a great tribute to Sir John A. Macdonald. It is one which is worthy of him and the contribution which he made to Canada.
I think that in this biography of Mr. Creighton's we have a precedent, which we hope will be emulated in the future by our writers and historians, whereby a very great and important source of history and of honouring our past traditions will be found. I think many of our heroes of history have not been sufficiently written about and reported upon, particularly in popular, readable histories of the style of Mr. Creighton's. I may say in this regard that having read this to a very large degree panegyric of Sir John A. by Mr. Creighton, I had a few qualms in doing a little research into the political affiliations of its author, and I thought possibly I would get a view from the other side. Subsequent to reading this biography I read Sir Richard Cartwright's biography of Sir John A., and if one treads a road between the two he might possibly achieve the true picture of Sir John A. I would not suggest to hon. members of the party of which the hon. member for Queens is a member that they would find the complete truth according to their liking in Sir Richard Cartwright's biography. The social graces of the attorney general for Canada west are given more preeminence in that biography than they are in the biography of Mr. Creighton.
With respect to honouring other days, there is only one remark of the hon. member's to which I would take exception, and that is the inference he drew that we honour St. Patrick's day and that St. Patrick's day in his view, I gathered from his remarks, should not have the honoured place that it does have in the annals of our celebrations. Coming from the Ottawa valley I must take great exception to any such suggestion. I would suggest to the hon. member that in honouring St. Patrick's day we do no less honour to Sir John A. Macdonald, except that we possibly honour St. Patrick's day with a little more revelry and a little more boisterously.
I would also point out with respect to the 1864 cavalcade to Charlottetown, which is being celebrated this year and which we sincerely hope will be celebrated with honour and broad acclaim throughout the nation- because it was certainly this meeting which ultimately led to confederation-that this was originally to be a meeting, as the hon. member for Queens no doubt knows far better than I, only to discuss maritime union. In fact, the meeting had virtually been abandoned when the members from Canada east and Canada west embarked on their jolly cruise, and the

meeting ultimately became one for confederation of all the colonies of British North America. I understand that the maritime papers in particular paid considerable tribute to the social graces not only of the attorney general for Canada west but to the many members who came from the parliament of Canada to Charlottetown, and their convivial ability to carouse well into the night was apparently one of the many reasons why the maritimers took so gleefully to the idea of confederation. May it be that this summer, when we are all celebrating that momentous event of the Charlottetown crusade, that we will enjoy the festivities as did our parliamentarians of those days.
I would point out in regard to the subject of our history generally that we have not paid sufficient heed or tribute to our history in the past, and there may be good reason for this. I think from the very nature of the diversity of our foundation, and by virtue of the fact that there were two basic founding races and languages at the root of our confederation, it may be that in the past-and I think politically this has been the case in the past-we tended to steer away from our history because that history would have pointed out the very differences that exist. There was a tendency to bury our heads in the sand like an ostrich and to say in the nonFrench parts of Canada: "We will study our history and you study yours, and never the twain shall meet". I think this is the reason we have paid insufficient heed to our history. We have not sufficiently glorified our heroes because we were, on both sides of the coin, afraid of the past.
I think that is the situation in which we find ourselves today it is self-evident that in fact this has been a tragedy, that we should have paid greater heed to our history. Perhaps the very differences of our foundation, had we come to know each other better through a more pervasive knowledge and wider acceptance of our respective histories and heroes, would have been resolved and made our foundation the stronger today. In this regard I have a few quotations which I think may be pertinent.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie) has very aptly brought before the house a quotation from Joseph Howe in regard to history. Here is something that Benjamin Disraeli said in the House of Commons in 1849:
The memory of a great name and the inheritance of a great example is the legacy of heroes.
I commend that thought to the house. Here again surely the memory of our heroes, such men as Sir John A. Macdonald who helped
Private Bills
to found this nation, would give a great inheritance and a great example to those who come after them, and should be better known.
I might say in this regard that we on this side of the house can take particular pride and honour in any suggestion to honour Sir John A. Macdonald because I think even those who know little history appreciate the fact that there would have been no confederation if George Brown had not made a very great personal sacrifice. Maurice Careless in his recent biography certainly gives credence to the belief that possibly Brown gave up his place in history to a very considerable degree by affiliating with Sir John A. Macdonald in the confederation movement. At that time it was the only thing that could be done to avoid the stalemate that existed, and certainly we would have had no Canada today had not Sir John A. and Sir George Brown worked together to bring about confederation.
I would also point to a quotation from Pliny the Younger found in book 5 of his "Epistles" where he says:
I hold it a noble task to reserve from oblivion those who deserve to be eternally remembered.
So I think we can see that historically all nations who have been worthy of the name and who have contributed something to the progress of mankind have heeded the admonition of Joseph Howe. On the other hand, we have those who decry the need for history and with whom I do not personally agree. But it may be of interest to the house to know that there are some who feel it is not necessarily important to record and honour the past in order to create a great nation. Among the great iconoclasts in this regard was Henry Ford, who said when he appeared as a witness at Mount Clemens, Michigan, when he was suing the Chicago Tribune in a libel suit in July, 1919, and I quote from the record of the trial: "History is bunk".
That may be, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that, bunk or no, it should be recorded and given a place of honour in our annals. Again, Thomas Jefferson said in his "Writings":
History in general is only as infamous as what is bad in government.
Thomas Carlyle said:
Happy the people whose annals are blank.
Montesquieu said:
Happy the people whose annals are tiresome.
Again, this view of history was probably summed up best by Schiller in his "Tablets" when he said:
How the best state to know? It is found out like the best woman-that least talked about.
According to these gentlemen the less you talk about your history the better it is, but I think most of us would decry this view and

Private Bills
accept the fact that what is very much needed in this country today is a greater appreciation and a wider knowledge of our history.
Not too long ago I had the pleasure to be in Washington during the Easter period, and I was very much impressed with the enthusiasm and the great thirst there is on the part of the people of the United States of America for their history and their past. One could not go to the Washington monument or the Lincoln memorial without coming away with a great awareness of the sincerity of the people of the United States, of their keen desire to know more about and feel their past and their history. Surely monuments such as these and also the Jefferson memorial in Washington are something we should think about very seriously.
When one sees thousands of boys and girls climbing the stairs or taking the elevator to the top of the Washington monument and then coming away with a deeper knowledge and appreciation of their past, when one sees in that great monument the contributions brick by brick and stone by stone by the various states, from various churches, from various groups throughout the length and breadth of that nation who have contributed funds and materials to that monument, he cannot but wish that we had memorials of this kind, great achievements in architecture and construction but, more than that, great achievements commemorating the past history of the United States and its heroes, which is something that we do not appear to have accomplished here.
I had the pleasure and honour of visiting the Lincoln memorial just at sunset and reading the second inaugural address which is completely inscribed on the walls of that great memorial. When one sees the figure of that great man with the second inaugural address facing it, one cannot help but reflect on the very great part that Abraham Lincoln played in their history and one cannot help but wish that we here in Ottawa had memorials to commemorate at least Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the same fashion, to the same degree and with the same dignity and exaltation that accompany the Washington monument and the Jefferson and Lincoln memorials in Washington.
True, we have memorials and statues. I think that the memorial chamber of the House of Commons is something we should all be proud of and cherish, but I think we need to do something on a wider scale and of greater stature, something to indicate that we are very proud of the heroes of our past, be they of French or Anglo Saxon origin, or be they of the other peoples who have contributed so greatly to this land. I think we

need to honour our past and our heroes more now that we have ever needed to before, because if this nation is to survive it can only survive if we appreciate our roots, if we appreciate our antecedents and if we take gladly now the very fact of our differences. If we try to hide our differences, if we are a little diffident about the fact that in our past we have different founding races and nationalities, then indeed we will not thrive and we may not even survive.
So, Mr. Speaker, may I commend the hon. member for the thought he has expressed in this bill. I take great honour in supporting the thought he has expressed. I should like to go a great deal farther than he has suggested. I believe the time is ripe not just to spend public moneys on bridges and other utilitarian things. If we have found out nothing else in the past two or three years, surely we have found that a nation does not survive by bridges, roads or public buildings alone which have utility as their only purpose. We need monuments. We need heroes. We need to look proudly at our roots of the past.
In supporting the hon. member's bill I suggest that not only should we have a Sir John A. Macdonald day, but that as a start in honouring our past history we should build here in Ottawa, the capital of this nation, the place where all people should come who wish to honour our history, two great memorials of the same stature and the same architecture as the Washington monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials. We should build two great memorials honouring Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Let us start from there and then let us build other monuments to our past so that all who come after us may be proud of the antecedents of this nation and of our past history.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened very closely to the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) and welcome indeed his support of Bill No. C-31. It is probably no surprise to any member of this house that I too wish to support this bill. Unlike those young people who have not yet heard of Sir John A. Macdonald, I cannot remember a time when I did not hear of him very frequently, if not daily. Sir John A. Macdonald is synonymous with Conservative, in fact, with Tory, and no matter how many times I am called a Tory I have always, however it is meant, taken it as a compliment. I am a Tory. However, it is quite obvious that that is not the reason I am supporting Bill No. C-31, an act respecting Sir John A. Macdonald day. It would not be reasonable to invest this bill with political overtones or party ambitions. It would seem to me to be an insult to our historical growth to do such a thing.

First of all, I would support it because I am sure of the basis of this bill, because of the character of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) who has introduced it. There is no more intelligent or sincere member in this house. He has not been known, to my knowledge, in this chamber or outside of it to make statements that have not been well thought out and always moderate. Second, I feel that in reaching this almost unbelievable standard of living that our country enjoys, in spite of our short age, our geography, our climate and our relatively small population, we have of necessity concentrated on material and physical demands. We must beware of neglecting the intangibles which would probably have come automatically through development under slower conditions of growth.
Every country has had its national figures and history is more meaningful, more real and more alive when we see it through personalities. Those who follow can identify themselves with other human beings in many different ways. It seems to me that this is the purest link with our past, with what may be unfamiliar and increasingly obscure as the years and the decades go by. Every Canadian should have a deep feeling for the process of compromise, conciliation, diplomacy and the enormous effort that went into the confederation of 1867. How better to develop this feeling than to set aside a day which will recall the successful results? By calling this day after Canada's first prime minister, we will also recognize a factor that must not be lost sight of in the dust of the political arena, and that is the factor that the office of prime minister warrants respect on all occasions. It is a permanent position not to be overridden by new theories or even by rebellions. Respect does not develop automatically. The respect accorded Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II has not come about by accident. Into it goes many years of attitudes, changing, maturing, sometimes weakening and sometimes strengthening.
Victoria day goes all the way back to 1845, and now incorporates Elizabeth II's birthday as well as that of the early Queen Victoria. Victoria day and Dominion day are really the only two of our nine statutory holidays that can be completely designated as historical. Although Remembrance day has a close connection with our national history, it is none the less more personal. That day our minds dwell most on the courage and service of Canadians and their individual and personal sacrifices.
It seems to me the time has come when we should guard the legends, the memories that deepen and strengthen in any country as the years go by. We can well afford at this time when our need for unity is so great, when
Private Bills
our desire for unity is so often expressed, to make every effort, take every possible step that will lead us in that direction. I feel that a national holiday named for our first prime minister would be good for Canada and good for Canadians. It would remind us of our history and our form of government in a pleasant, relaxed way. Citizens need not always be reminded of government by taxes, ponderous speeches or by the political thrust and cut, which is sometimes tiresome to those who do not follow it closely.
Let us give Canadians a holiday by means of this act, thereby reminding ourselves that, overriding the problems that come and go in any country, is the fact that we are glad that confederation took place in 1867. We are glad that we have a system of government headed by a prime minister, and all that that means in protection against rigidity, against oppression and rule by force.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable hesitation that I follow the outstanding contributions made by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie), the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) and the gracious lady member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Cassel-man). I want to say that I am wholly in sympathy with the aims of the hon. member for Queens, namely that we should do more to protect the records of our past and to see to it that all Canadians are aware of the accomplishments of the statesmen who helped, as a team, to make Canada possible. I am not sure that I would be wholly in accord with the idea of a holiday specifically set aside as John A. Macdonald day. Certainly this prime minister, our first, was a remarkable Canadian and a man who contributed a tremendous amount to the development of the nation.
I thought perhaps one of his greatest accomplishments, and I am not sure I wholly applaud it, was the fact he was able to break the back of Nova Scotia's opposition to confederation by enticing Joseph Howe into the federal cabinet in 1869. I am not just sure how that was accomplished. There have been suggestions from time to time that the social graces that were mentioned at an earlier stage of this debate may have had something to do with that accomplishment. It was said by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on June 8, 1891, at the time of the death of Sir John A. Macdonald, that Sir John A. Macdonald now belongs to the ages and that it could be said with certainty the career that had just closed was one of the most remarkable careers of the century. I think this tribute from Sir Wilfrid is the measure of the mark Sir John A. Macdonald made on Canada.

Business of the House
While he has been one of the truly great Canadians of the past, I suggest that we must find a way somewhat between the neglect of the past for public figures and the extreme cult of the personality with regard to historic figures that has been shown in the United States and some other areas. We must find a middle path. We must find recognition for all of the great statesmen and prime ministers that followed John A. Macdonald I think that that recognition cannot be best found necessarily in national holidays. I feel that at the present time our July 1 holiday is a holiday that marks the memory of John A. Macdonald, Laurier, Joseph Howe and of all of those men collectively in something like a typically Canadian approach to our memory of the past.
I believe that our broadcasting systems, radio and television, and our schools could do far more than has been done in the past toward honouring the memory of our great men. Some of us had occasion, a year or two ago, to see a documentary on C.B.C. television concerning the life of Joseph Howe. It showed only the picture of a man that was a bit on the seedy side at the end of his career. It showed little of the greatness of Joseph Howe or his accomplishments. Coming from a province that has sent forward as prime ministers Sir Robert Borden, Sir John Thompson and Sir Charles Tupper, and a province which educated Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, I must say that I feel all these men and many others who served this nation should be recognized by the publication of concise and readable biographies. If necessary, government action should be taken to commission a number of concise biographies which could then be part of the curriculum of the schools of our country. I suggest this plan, if it would not be considered an invasion of provincial rights. Certainly, there is a great deal that can be done in that direction. I know of nothing that puts it better than the words that were read by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) in which Joseph Howe said that it was the wise nation that preserved its record.
