The money available to the corporation is used much in the nature of a revolving fund. Principal repaid by farmers which in the last year amounted to about $25.5 million is available for re-lending, thus reducing the net amount the corporation must borrow from the Minister of Finance.
As I indicated a moment ago, because of the increased lending in recent years the present funds are not going to be enough to meet the needs of farmers this summer. The corporation has commitments to the Minister of Finance or to farmers in the form of loan approvals of about $378 million. This leaves only $22 million, besides principal repayments by farmers who already have loans, to cover new loan commitments. Based on current demands for loans and the rate of repayment on existing loans by farmers it is estimated that the additional $200 million in funds which this bill proposes to make available should be enough to keep the corporation in loan funds until late in 1966.
Before discussing the other amendments to the Farm Credit Act which are proposed by this bill I would like to point out that these are not all the changes we are considering in farm credit legislation. Because of all the changes taking place on farms, changes are taking place in the requirements for farm credit programs. The federal government is involved in farm credit in various ways. The Department of Veterans Affairs through the Veterans Land Act administration provides credit to full-time and part-time farmers who 20220-245*
qualify as a result of military service. Intermediate term credit is available to farmers through loans from the chartered banks guaranteed by the government under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The Department of Forestry in administering the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act is also vitally interested in farm credit, and the use of credit in furthering its programs. All the provinces are also involved one way or another in providing credit to farmers.
For all these reasons we have decided that there is a need for co-ordinated study and research in this field to provide a basis for a more comprehensive farm credit policy which will take into consideration all forms of credit needed by farmers.
We want to find out where the gaps are in existing credit facilities and what role should be assigned to each of the various agencies in the farm credit field. We have, therefore, established an interdepartmental committee on farm credit. It is under the chairmanship of the director general of my department's economic branch. It has representation from the Veterans Land Act administration, the Department of Finance, the Department of Forestry and the Farm Credit Corporation. It has been established on a continuing basis. Its function is to appraise the total credit needs of Canadian agriculture, arrange for studies and research for that purpose, and consider and report on submissions and representations to the government about farm credit matters. From its appraisal of credit requirements this continuing committee on

Farm, Credit Act
farm credit will make recommendations to the Minister of Agriculture about existing farm credit services and any new services considered necessary for the proper development of Canadian agriculture.
One of its first responsibilities will be to consider and recommend ways in which the provinces and the committee might best cooperate to ensure that federal farm credit policies are co-ordinated with the programs and the needs of individual provinces. We recognize that existing farm credit programs are doing a good job for farmers within their respective bounds. But I believe this committee will provide the basis for bringing about greater co-ordination of existing programs and ensure that we keep right on top of new credit problems arising from the dynamic changes now taking place in agriculture. In the meantime, however, there are new farm credit needs which must be met now, and in the legislation proposed in this bill we are trying to meet them in so far as they refer to long term mortgage credit.
The Farm Credit Corporation recently reviewed government sponsored farm credit programs in 11 principal agricultural countries. It has made a more detailed study of two national farm credit services in the United States, and it has also made a survey of a cross-section of 2,600 Canadian farmers, to see just what their present uses of credit are, what they think they will need in the immediate future, and any shortcomings they think exist in present services. The complete results of this survey are not yet available, but it has already been shown that many of the farmers consulted felt that existing limits on loans from the corporation are too low. So we want to move on this now. We want to do everything we can to make sure the corporation fulfils its role in the long term mortgage credit field.
Since the corporation started its operations in 1959 the percentage of farmers taking maximum loans has gradually increased. In the last fiscal year 11.3 per cent of those who borrowed under part II obtained maximum loans of $20,000, and 15.6 per cent of those borrowing under part III took maximum loans of $27,500. In other words, about 1,000 farmers last year borrowed the maximum amount available to them under the Farm Credit Act. In many cases these maximum loans were not enough to meet the farmers' needs for long term mortgage credit. As a result, instead of having long term loans to carry debts which should have been carried by long term loans, many farmers had to carry this type of debt on short term, or intermediate term loans, often at interest rates much higher than the corporation's or, for that matter, at rates much higher than

would be considered an economic or unsubsidized rate of interest for the corporation. There has also been an increasing number of farmers operating good family farm units who have not borrowed from the corporation because the present maximum loans would not have been enough to meet their minimum needs.
Canadian farmers have established an excellent record with the Farm Credit Corporation. They have shown that they know how to use credit to increase the efficiency and productivity of their farms; they have shown a willingness to use good advice from the corporation, and they have also shown a willingness and an ability to repay their loans. If we are going to make it possible for them to go on producing more efficiently and to improve their standards of living, and in doing so to continue improving their service to the Canadian consumer and the general economy of the country, then I believe we have got to do everything we can to ensure that they can get the credit they need.
The present limits are $20,000 under part II of the act, which covers standard loans not supervised by the corporation, and $27,500 for loans under part III of the act, which covers loans that are supervised by the corporation. Hon. members know, of course, that the maximum term in each case is 30 years. Rapid changes have taken place in agriculture since that time and it is evident that the present limits on loans are no longer adequate to establish efficient, viable family farms in many sectors of Canadian agriculture. By doubling the size of the loans, as proposed in this bill, the government believes an important step will be taken toward improving the corporation's capacity to help farmers in the way they need help and in a way that enables them to help themselves. That is the kind of help all our farmers want-a chance to make the best possible use of their time and energy and the resources of their farms. I want to point out also that the proposed increase in the maximum loans obviously will not prevent the corporation from continuing to make small loans to those farmers who do not need or want big loans.
Now I would like to say a few words about interest rates. Hon. members will be aware that the royal commission on banking and finance has recommended that loans made by the corporation should be at an economic rate of interest. The present statutory limit of 5 per cent is, in effect, an uneconomic or subsidized rate. The present cost of money to the corporation, based on a 20 year term, is 51 per cent, and the cost of administration was a little less than 1 per cent during the past fiscal year. The government recognizes,

however, that the primary objective of credit from the corporation is to help farmers to build up their farms to an efficient economic size so that they will have an adequate standard of living and be able to repay their loans.
We have taken the position that in order to assist the smaller farmer to expand his enterprise to economic size and improve his standard of living we should be willing to provide him with the required credit up to the amounts available under the Farm Credit Act at the present time at a rate of 5 per cent. However, when the farmer borrows amounts above the present limits, we believe it would be reasonable that he should pay for this additional money at an economic rate which will vary, of course, from time to time according to the cost of money to the corporation. I might say here that this economic rate is the price that the federal government will have to pay for money. It is proposed that this rate will be fixed by the corporation, subject to approval by the governor in council, and will not be more than the interest charged to the corporation for this money, the cost of administration and a reasonable reserve against loss.
I do not believe farmers will object to paying this economic rate. They are getting this additional capital now at costs much higher than will be charged them by the corporation, and on terms which are much less satisfactory to them. Many farmers have said, "Make the credit available to us so that we can establish good, efficient farming enterprises, and we will pay the interest rate that is required". The additional cost, when spread over a number of years, will certainly be less than the additional income the farmers will be able to earn by getting this additional credit on proper terms.
Some of the other amendments proposed, while they may not seem significant at first glance, can be of real importance in the operation of the corporation. One amendment will make it possible for the corporation to lend to the executor or administrator of an estate of a deceased farmer, and thus the corporation will be able to assist the farmers' heirs to continue to operate and develop their farms, even though the estate may not yet be fully settled. Another amendment will make it possible for a father or an uncle to borrow money to assist a son or nephew or other relative to buy a farm. This particular amendment will be of great assistance to the corporation in its efforts to establish young men in farming. Many of these young men being started in farming obtain loans under part III of the act. As the act now stands, when a farmer borrows money under part III, part of the loan is secured by chattels and that part must be repaid within ten years. This
Farm Credit Act
means that payments during the first years of the loan, when the young man has the least equity and the least income and is trying to develop his farm, run as much as 30 pex cent higher than they are during later years. So we are proposing that the corporation^ be permitted to amortize a loan under part III of the act throughout the entire 30 years. This will eliminate the large payments during the early years while the young farmer is struggling to build up his farm. This particular proposal will make it much easier for farmers just getting started.
I think we would do all farmers a favour in considering this bill if we remembered that the Farm Credit Act is intended to serve only the long term credit field. Intermediate term credit for the purchase of livestock, machinery and other such purposes is provided for under other legislation and we can discuss these other credit problems when such other legislation is before the house for consideration. I would not wish to leave the impression that the present bill represents all the changes we will eventually want to make in the operations of the Farm Credit Corporation. The government is concerned, and I am sure hon. members are concerned, about the welfare of those farmers who are unable to qualify for loans under the Farm Credit Act, either because of the limited production from then-farms or because they do not have the required equity.
The Farm Credit Corporation has done a lot to assist the small farmer to enlarge his unit to the point where he can make a good living for himself and his family. About 45 per cent of the money lent by the corporation last year went to help farmers to buy more land. Unfortunately, there are many faced with problems which credit by itself will not solve. Others who want to start farming, and have not the capital they need to get going, could not afford to borrow and pay back all the money needed to buy a good farm together with the livestock and equipment, particularly with the price of land in some parts of Canada today.
To solve these and other problems of a similar nature requires the co-ordination of the resources of several agencies. We need to get all of the people who are involved in agricultural development to work together to develop and to apply the policies and programs to get at the roots of the problems.
One of the principal purposes of the farm credit study committee we have set up will be to determine how credit can best be used as one of the means to assist these people. As the committee's work gets under way we can expect further improvements in our program

Farm Credit Act
to help farmers. Meanwhile, the amendments proposed by this bill will do a lot to improve the capacity of the corporation to reinforce and strengthen the family farm in Canadian agriculture. They are amendments which we believe are needed right now. I think there is a lot to be said for doing everything we can to keep the family farm. As the communist countries have learned all too well, there is nothing like the pride of ownership to encourage a farmer to do his best. After all, why should he not do his best when he knows he is doing it for himself? But besides the obvious benefits to all Canadians that arise from this pride of ownership on our farms, there is the feeling of independence and self-reliance which farmers get from working for themselves. This is something which cannot be measured in dollars and cents, but I do not think any hon. member would argue that it is not a very valuable extra commodity that this country gets from its farmers.
This measure, Mr. Speaker, is in two parts. We are now considering the farm credit bill, and then there is the administrative side of the act. The annual report of the Farm Credit Corporation is now in the hands of the queen's printer and we will be tabling it in the house before the end of June. If hon. members wish to question the administration we would be quite happy to have this report referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization for consideration. The officials of the corporation would welcome this opportunity to discuss the administration of the Farm Credit Act with the agriculture committee in the hope that improvements may be made, because hon. members represent the different views and problems of all of the provinces. We are trying all the time to improve the administration of the act, and I think this would be an opportunity for hon. members to bring forward their ideas on the administration of the act. I spoke to the manager of the corporation this evening and he said he would welcome the opportunity to have this report before the committee where we could probably learn a great deal more. In the last few months we have been able to cut the time for servicing these loans by days. At the moment we are lending something like $1 million a day and we have about $22 million left. Some days it is a little more than that, but I am sure hon. members can see the urgency of getting the bill approved by the house so that credit to the farmers is not held up.

Farm Credit Act
I am convinced that over a 10 year period, the Farm Credit Corporation can, with a 5 per cent rate, meet its obligations without having to be subsidized by the federal government and the Department of Agriculture.
Moreover, even if the Minister of Agriculture grants a subsidy of a few hundred thousand dollars for the farm credit administration, that is worthwhile because this legislation enables our farmers to organize their farms on a basis which gives them a decent living.
There are improvements in the legislation now under study. For instance, we see that apiculture will be included in the description of the word agriculture; this new description which extends the meaning of the word agriculture will be accepted by several persons as an improvement. But it will be necessary for the Farm Credit Corporation to pay special attention to those who will apply for a loan, because we must not forget that agriculture, in certain area, operates on a commercial basis.
Moreover, there are in this legislation changes concerning loans under Part III of the act. Formerly, an amount of money was loaned and had to be repaid within 10 years. With this new legislation, authority is given to spread the repayment over a 30 year period.
Looking at that, a question immediately comes to mind which I should like the minister to answer. That question will also be asked by all farmers already having a loan under part III. What will happen to those who already have been granted a loan by the Farm Credit Corporation and who have to pay back the amount, under part III, on a 10 year basis? Will the Farm Credit Corporation be authorized to extend those payments from a 10 year to a 30 year period?
No reply was given to that question, that is, in his statement the minister did not deal with this aspect of the question. So, on the farmers' behalf, I ask him to consider the possibility of having those borrowers benefit from that amendment and placed on an equal footing with the new ones who will be entitled to pay back their loans under part III over a 30 year period.
Mr. Speaker, although we are discussing this evening the first amendment to a piece of legislation introduced by the previous government, I find once again that there are not too many Liberal members in the house. The fact is to be noted, because each time we speak of agriculture, each time we are dealing with a farm problem, the same thing happens. Our good friends the Liberals show little interest.
That is not true.
If you wish, we shall figure out how many government members there are in the house now.

speechtext: Order. I should like to call the hon. member to order by asking him not to stray from the subject now before us.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, I wish to point out that my remarks fall within the limits of this debate because we are discussing a very important measure, and if our friends the Liberals do not want to discuss it or hear about it, it is because they are not interested in the part this government must play to help agriculture in Canada, especially in eastern Canada-

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. In my opinion, what the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) is saying is entirely incorrect. Nothing could show better the interest the Liberal members take in agriculture than the fact that we are studying tonight an excellent bill introduced by the government. Therefore, agriculture is close to our hearts.

I thank the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) for saying that this is an excellent bill, because it is simply the logical follow-up to the legislation we passed in 1959. That is partly the reason why I pointed out that there are only 16 Liberal members in the house; I wanted the hon. member for Lotbiniere to rise and praise the merits of this act passed by the Conservative government in 1959.

Would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member wants to be fair to his colleagues. He must read the papers and he knows very well that most Liberal members are attending a banquet tonight. Therefore, I ask him to show his colleagues the same respect we have for the members of his party when they have party meetings.
Is that a question or a statement?

I thank the hon. member for calling my attention to the fact that tonight 116 Liberal members are attending the banquet of the Liberal federation and are, therefore, more interested in Liberal banquets than in agriculture.
Just like you, when you have meetings.

Now, Mr. Speaker, we will have the opportunity of examining the bill thoroughly, section by section.

As I said, we approve of several of the proposed amendments since they will improve the legislation enacted in 1959.
Yet, we will have criticism to offer concerning other amendments such as the possibility of charging more than 5 per cent interest on certain agricultural loans.
Members of our group advocate the establishment of a uniform 5 per cent interest rate. We feel the federal government can authorize the Farm Credit Corporation to grant loans to Canadian farmers at no more than 5 per cent interest.
We would also ask the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) to consider the possibility of providing in the legislation that existing loans, which were granted under part 3 of the act and which are to be repaid within ten years, be revised in such a way that those borrowers may be on the same footing as those who borrow from the corporation in the future.
A while ago the minister stated that the official report of the Farm Credit Corporation will be referred to the agriculture committee after its publication. We welcome that announcement because corporation officials will surely be in a position to give us information which will be useful not only to hon. members but also to all farmers in Canada. However, before accepting the minister's proposal outright, I must tell him that the committee on agriculture must first of all study the question of feed grain before tackling any other matters.
To conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said at the beginning. We shall approve Bill C-100 with some reservations, as I pointed out earlier.

Mr. Speaker, this is a most important piece of legislation, which will affect the lives of a good many Canadian farmers across the country, their families, the communities in which they live and the nation as a whole. I rise on behalf of this party to support the principle of the bill. We will have some suggestions to make in respect of one or two amendments when we get into committee of the whole. But, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays). Knowing of his firm belief that free enterprise should extend from here to eternity, I wish to congratulate him for introducing this socialistic piece of legislation which gives effect to socialist philosophy as preached by this group throughout the years, to the extent that it provides for co-operation between the government and individual farmers by way of long term low interest loans to the advantage of the government, 20220-246
Farm Credit Act
to the advantage of the farmer and to the advantage of the state. This is the gospel that we preached in this house ever since this party was formed. I sincerely congratulate the minister. Honestly, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if the minister were in this house for 40 years he would finally apply for membership in our party.
This party, as its predecessor the C.C.F., has for many years urged the need for long term low interest loans to farmers. There is quite a long history of long term low interest loans in European agriculture. However, it has only been developed in satisfactory form in recent years in Canada. I remember well that I made my first speech on behalf of this party on this subject in 1945. It has taken a long time for this party and farmers organizations to create a public climate that would affect the opinion of old line parties in this house to the extent that we saw this legislation introduced initially by the former government.
For years farmers organizations across Canada have been urging the need for this type of legislation. For years we have known that the private credit sources could not meet the need, would not accept their responsibility, would not provide loans for a sufficient length of time, would not provide loans at low enough interest and would not condition those loans with satisfactory security for the farmers' tenure. I cannot help mentioning at this time that I am sure there are a good many people in Saskatchewan who rejoiced when a C.C.F. government was elected there and prevented the private lending agencies from collaring their farms because they were behind in their payments a year or two as a result of poor crops and low prices.
And they rejoiced when it went out.

I hear some muttering from the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson). Honestly, I believe that is a most unkind remark coming from one who is entitled to prefix his name with the word "Reverend".
As a result of this agitation years ago, as a result of the agitation of the old progressive party, which had an influence on the Liberal government of the day and which was later absorbed by the Liberal party, the old Canadian farm loan board was established and functioned for many years. It was an improvement over the previous years, but the legislation was too restrictive and the administration of the act was too rigid. I can illustrate this by citing several cases in my own constituency. I am thinking at the present time of one farmer who made application

Farm Credit Act
to the old Canadian farm loan board on three occasions for a loan. All he received was a letter from New Westminster-nobody visited his farm-informing him that the area in which he lived was not a suitable area for farming, would not provide a satisfactory security for a loan, and so on. On his first application to the Farm Credit Corporation he received a loan in the amount for which he asked, $17,500, and he is doing well now.
This shows the improvement in the act passed by the last government. I admit freely that these amendments are a further improvement of that act. Now, a lot of the research, shall I say, in connection with the problem was done under the Veterans Land Act by the Veterans Land Act administration. I think we should give them credit. They had an opportunity, because of the nature of the legislation which was given effect shortly after the conclusion of the second world war, and they made good use of it. For the first time we had loans on a certain basis and counselling from the administrators of the Veterans Land Act. I think we should pay particular tribute to the work done by Brigadier General J. T. Rutherford, who was chairman of the Veterans Land Act administration, the vice chairman, Mr. G. Owen, the senior officials and the officials in the country.
I would say that I have had quite a long experience in dealing with farm problems, the farmers' need for credit and that sort of thing. I can tell you that my family needed it. If it had not been for relatives dying in the old country we could have starved to death at one time. We could not get credit at that time, but circumstances are somewhat different now. These gentlemen were pioneers in this field, and this new approach to farm credit took advantage of the experience gained by the administration of that act when they not only did research at the head office but co-operated with the officials in the field.
I do want to mention what I think should be considered the lending policy bible. It was prepared by the two officials I have just mentioned. I believe it is an excellent document and I think every member of this house should keep a copy in his files and refer to it. Mind you, the situation will change as we acquire additional experience and the results of more research into this problem, but I do think this publication lays the foundation for the philosophy of farm credit in Canada. I wish to quote briefly from this book which deals extensively with the whole question. Dealing with lending policy, it says:
The Farm Credit Act, which was proclaimed on October 5, 1959, replaced the Canadian Farm Loan Act. It set up the Farm Credit Corporation, reporting to parliament through the Minister of
[Mr. Herridge.j
Agriculture, to take over from the Canadian farm loan board which had reported through the Minister of Finance.
I think that was a wise improvement. When administration is in the hands of a minister of finance the approach is different from that which becomes evident when administration is in the hands of a minister of agriculture-and I am not blaming ministers of finance. They, naturally, concentrate on an entirely businesslike approach whereas a minister of agriculture is in touch with farm requirements and farm organizations. When the minister of agriculture of that day was introducing this legislation he defined its object as follows:
To assist Canadian farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into economic family farm units, each of which will be of sufficient size to produce, under the operation of the owner, the farm income necessary to meet all operating and maintenance costs, provide an adequate livelihood for the owner-operator and his dependants, and retire any required credit, with interest, within an appropriate term.
I think this is a good definition of the economic family farm unit. All that is required for its success is, first, good land, then markets, and then long term loans at low interest to be repaid out of the production of the farm. The publication goes on to deal with the part this legislation will play in rural development and the author mentions that the legislation is a calculated risk. He says:
There is no doubt that in bringing down the Farm Credit Act when it did, and in its present form, the government was relying to a very considerable degree on its being efficiently and fearlessly administered in line with its objective of helping to create economic units suitable to, and which could operate profitably in, each agricultural area of the country. This is your job and mine. It is a big responsibility, a great trust, and an inspiring challenge.
Fie goes on to assert that farmers should he informed of their rights under the act. I think this is a wise observation. Then he deals with the initial interview in connection with counselling, and indicates situations in which loans would not appear to be indicated and situations in which loans would appear to be indicated. Later, he discusses administration in general, and finally he winds up the preamble to this excellent publication by noting the need for co-operation. He states:
It is most important, therefore, that there be close liaison and co-operation between the corporation at head office, branch and field levels and these other agencies at concurrent levels in order that we may be of mutual assistance to one another in the attainment of a common over-all objective.
Then he urges co-operation between the different branches of the government service, the farm press and radio, national farm

organizations and their branches, the Veterans Land Act administration, the extension services of the provincial department of agriculture, provincial farm credit agencies and agricultural colleges, faculties and schools. Further on, he deals with the need for public relations. Once again, I wish to say that this is an excellent resume of the basic philosophy of farm credit as applied to Canadian conditions.
Although the act as it now stands is an excellent piece of legislation, the farm organizations, as a result of changing conditions and new experience ever since 1959, have been urging amendments and I wish to quote briefly from a speech made by president J. M. Bentley of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island on January 21. This is what he had to say:
In the field of farm credit, I would like to pay tribute to the work of the Farm Credit Corporation. It has been instrumental in enabling many farmers to secure economic farm units and has ensured a higher standard of living for many farm families. However, not all the problems of farm credit can be met by the Farm Credit Corporation as it exists today. Agriculture is changing so rapidly through mechanization that the credit needs of farmers are changing as well. I would like to suggest that we should consider establishing means of thinking the problem through by study and analysis and arriving at new and sound proposals. There are a number of areas in which farm credit needs are not now being adequately met:
1.	Loan limits are probably inadequate under present conditions.
He mentioned this need first, and I see that the request is now being met in the amendments proposed in this bill. The list continues:
2.	Adequate arrangements for meeting the problem of transfer of farms on the retirement, or death, of the present owners.
I have personal knowledge of a number of cases where this type of amendment is needed.
3.	Operating, or intermediate credit needs, are not being adequately met by the farm improvement loan program or the present banking system.
We are looking forward to amendments to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Then the president goes on to deal with the need for emergency or disaster credit which, I trust, the minister is considering. I am one of those who believe that a disaster suffered by a farmer as a result of floods or other natural agency should be borne by all of us, not by the individual alone, and this could be done at very slight cost to the nation or to the farm population as a whole. Then, Mr. Bentley continues:
In the study and analysis of the above areas, the advisory committee of the Farm Credit Corporation should be given more status and authority so that it can perform a most useful and im-
20220-246J
Farm Credit Act
portant function. The advisory committee should not merely confine its activities to matters arising under the act or to matters referred to it by the minister, or the corporation. It should be able to initiate study into the legislation itself and be able to advise the corporation on emerging problems and needs as they arise from time to time.
I read that paragraph because I should like the minister to comment on this suggestion by the president of the federation of agriculture. I judge from conversations I have had with farmers and with officers of local farm organizations that there is great merit in the suggestion. It is one which I think could be put into effect simply by means of administrative changes; there would be no need for any alteration in the legislation, and no doubt this will come about as a result of the minister's more socialistic approach to life.
As I said earlier, the purpose of this legislation was to maintain, improve and develop the economic family farm unit in Canada. Before concluding, I would suggest that changing circumstances in the future will lead to further amendments being required-[DOT] changes in administrative forms, and so on. I believe there is a great need for continued research on the part of officials of the corporation and the related agencies of the federal and provincial governments, in order that we may make these adjustments from year to year if necessary so as to make the act as satisfactory and as useful as possible. I noticed an article in the current issue of the Family Herald. I am a simple sort of soul-
Hear, hear.
Explain.

-and I enjoy reading farm publications. I enjoy reading the letters from people asking how they can cure mam-mitis in dairy cows, or asking how they can solve some legal problems. These are all human problems to me. I am sure the minister reads them as well and I am sure he would be a very excellent person to answer these questions. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, there is an article in the Family Herald of June 4, which publication came on my desk just today. I notice that these farm publications are getting like the others now; they are issued before the date they are supposed to be published. However, Mr. Speaker, this article is entitled "Credit. One economist: Banks don't know farm needs". I shall quote from this article because I think it is worth while:
For the bulk of Canada's farmers the higher ceilings for Farm Credit Corporation loans asked for in agriculture minister Harry Hays' first measure before Commons will not make much difference. Only 13 per cent of farmers who have received F.C.C. loans so far qualified for the present maximums of $20,000 and $27,000. F.C.C. officials estimate that only some 80,000 or 90,000 of

Farm Credit Act
Canada's farmers will be able to take advantage of the bigger loans when the present ceilings are doubled.
I think that is a pretty healthy number, to start with. The article continues:
The new amendments fall into line with one of the recommendations of the royal commission on banking and finance: That with the high cost of farms today present F.C.C. ceilings simply are not high enough to ease the transfer of many of our farms from one generation to another. The amendments would increase the ceiling on part II loans from $20,000 to $40,000 and on part III loans (for younger farmers under supervision) from $27,000 to $55,000.
The whole question of farm credit has been under review for some time by F.C.C. and departmental offices.
Then this article goes on to indicate the need for continuing studies in this direction. This, Mr. Speaker, is a farm journal indicating that these private sources of credit are simply inadequate under present circumstances. Before concluding I wish to say a word with respect to public relations. I do think that everything possible should be done to inform the farm organizations and the farmers of the terms of this act, its administration and the requirements that have to be met to qualify for loans, and so on. On occasion I have met farmers who were quite uninformed in this respect. I have just been informed by my colleague to my rear that the minister is now writing a weekly column. 1 had overlooked that. I suggest that the farmers, when they read the publications for which he is writing, could be informed through that column. The farmers organizations and other organizations should be kept well informed in this regard.
Perhaps your colleague could use his column.

I find that in this type of society these people are too segregated anyway. One finds a small town or village surrounded by a farming community, and very often the organizations have no idea of the detail of this type of legislation and how it is being administered to serve the farmers and producers of the area. I suggest that the officials of the minister's department could very well take time out now and again to give talks, on this and other subjects relating to agriculture, to farm organizations and other organizations in the towns and cities around the countryside that are concerned with agriculture. These talks could be given to Rotary clubs, chambers of commerce, labour organizations, and so on. I suggest it would be a good idea for the minister's officials to make a point of talking to some of the meetings of local labour organizations and letting them know of the farmers' problems and what the government of Canada is doing in an effort to
XMr. Herridge.]
meet these problems. The more we understand one another's problems, the more we will march together. I am a firm believer in this respect, Mr. Speaker, in so far as the differences that are supposed to exist between Quebec and the rest of Canada are concerned. These differences are supposed to be very sharp indeed. When the young hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) has spoken he has sometimes said some quite unpleasant things from my point of view; but actually he is a thoroughly decent type when you get to know him. The point is, you must get to know him.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that this information can be given through farm periodicals and the press in general. This is about all I am going to say at this time. We will have some comments to make on the various clauses of the bill when we are in committee, and we propose to introduce one or two minor amendments in an effort to improve it somewhat, particularly the lowering of the interest rate to 5 per cent so that it is 5 per cent across the board. In conclusion I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for the introduction of these amendments, which we in this group consider to be another step forward in the march toward a Canadian co-operative commonwealth.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every member of this house wants the farm units in Canada to be economical. We take the position, as has been stated by other hon. members of this house from time to time, that land values are continuing to rise, that machinery prices are continually going up, and therefore for farmers to maintain, or first of all establish, economic units it is necessary for the amount of available credit to be increased in line with these increased costs. I want to say at the outset that there are a number of amendments to the Farm Credit Act included in this bill, but I suggest that the main one is to increase the maximum amounts available.
I want to say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and to the government that simply increasing the limits-the maximum limits, if I can put it that way-to an individual farmer is not going to solve all the problems respecting farm credit. As the Minister of Agriculture pointed out earlier this evening, and as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) repeated, only some 13 per cent of the loans granted now are for the maximum amount available. In my experience in discussing this matter of credit with farmers, the limits have been part of the problem in their view, but in addition to that there are many other regula-

tions and points of administration that require review and amendment as well.
Dr. J. C. Gilson, associate professor of agricultural economics of the University of Manitoba, made a rather exhaustive study of farm credit and farm credit requirements in 1958. He had this to say:
Farm credit is a two-edged sword, make no mistake about that. Used wrongly it can cause grief and financial disaster. On the other hand, credit can be one of the most powerful "tools" of production in modem farming. It takes money to make money, and credit is frequently the starting point.
I want to agree with many of the assertions the Minister of Agriculture made this evening, particularly with respect to the matter of increasing the limits from $20,000 to $40,000 under one part of the act and from $27,000 to a maximum of $55,000 under another part.
There are, as I said at the outset, a number of other measures. Dr. Gilson points out six of these problems which arose in 1958, many of which are just as valid today because the legislation which has been passed through this house and the consequent amendments have not in fact met the problem. In the first place, he says it is practically impossible to estimate the number of farmers who need credit at the present time. There are several types of situations, however, where it is safe to assume that greatly increased amounts of farm credit are needed. The first item he lists is the situation where a father transfers his farming business to his son-in other words, the family farm. Dr. Gilson points out that in this area there was practically no legislation in 1958 to deal with this very serious problem of farm families losing their equity in the family farm owing to a death in the family and a transfer having to be made. The bill before us tonight meets this problem to some extent because it does allow for the administrator of an estate to carry on and have credit made available to him, so that the land and other assets do not have to be sold.
In addition to that another amendment allows a borrower to acquire farmland or to advance money to a son-in-law, daughter or other relative. I think that is a very important improvement. As a matter of fact, the province of Alberta recognized this question of transfers within the family in 1959 and brought in an act specifically designed to take care of such matters when a father had reached retirement age, and so on. I think that what is in the bill is definitely a step in the right direction, although the bill does not go far enough. The reason I say that is because the major responsibility for farm credit rests with the federal government rather than provincial governments. We all know that under the constitution of Canada the federal
Farm Credit Act
government is charged with, and given full responsibility for, the control of currency, credit and matters dealing with monetary and fiscal policies in the nation. I think farm credit is primarily one of such activities. Whenever any of the provinces have needed to move in the direction of farm credit it is because the federal government has failed to recognize the need and to pass legislation to fulfil that need.
I believe there are at least four general considerations which should be taken into account in arriving at a sound credit policy for the Canadian farmers. First of all-and this is provided for partly but not completely-there should be provision made for supervised credit primarily for young farmers in low income families. We know there are many very ambitious and capable young men who have the talent to go into the business of farming as a lifetime occupation but are unable to do so because there is not enough credit available for them at the outset to set up an economic farm unit. The raising of the maximum limit alone will not solve this problem.
Another matter not dealt with by the bill is that debt repayment schedules should be tied to rises and falls in farm incomes. I think that most members from the rural areas will agree with me when I say that quite often, in fact in the majority of cases, loans made to farmers are spread over a 20 or 30 years period. There are only a limited number of years when the annual income falls below that level which makes it impossible for him to meet the loan repayments and interest, and it is in that limited number of years that the farmer gets into difficulty. What happens is that he is usually forced to go to other markets and lending institutions outside the Farm Credit Corporation and farm improvement loans legislation and borrow money, not only to carry on his operation but also to meet the required repayments as well. I think there should be some provision made to make it possible to extend the term of repayment by one year when a farmer's income in one year drops below his ability to make the payments required.
I also think it is desirable that the complete financing of farm units be undertaken by one lender. For example, Dr. Gilson says that farms should be financed as a whole unit in contrast to a piecemeal approach. Under the terms of the Farm Credit Act and the farm improvements loans legislation it is possible, or will be when this bill passes, to borrow up to $55,000 both for farm equipment and for land. If we are to make this farm credit administration comprehensive and complete, there should be some provision in the act for these disastrous years, when a

Farm Credit Act
farmer is simply unable out of his current income to make the payments he is obliged to make for those years. Quite often these secondary loans, if I may call them that, are taken at substantially higher rates of interest, which only adds to his burden further down the road. I say that because I think that if arrangements were made for these disaster years it would keep the security for the loan made by the Farm Credit Corporation in better standing. With a secondary loan the farmer would be saddled at some later time with higher interest rates and would find them difficult to meet.
I agree with increasing the amount of loans so as to keep pace with the increasing price of land, farm equipment and so on.
The reason I urge the minister and the government to take into consideration this matter of providing some provision for these bad years is because I think, if we look at farm land values over the years, we see we really do not have depreciation at all. In fact, if history is to repeat itself for the next 20.years concerning what we have had during the past 20 years, there will be an appreciation or an increase in the values of all farm land, rather than depreciation, and no one is going to be able to run away with a farm. If the Farm Credit Corporation takes security in a farm, that farm will be there. The dollar value of the farm will be higher, five years after a loan is made, than it is at the time the loan is actually made.
I think the government should also give consideration to increasing the percentage of loan available in relation to the appraised value because, as I pointed out, the farm is there. It consists of land and is a very solid and substantial security. Also, Mr. Speaker, I think that some of the methods and the values that are allowed at this time respecting land are completely out of line with the market price.
We know that F.C.C. and other lenders are very conservative in their appraising of land values, and in many cases when a young farmer is getting started, if he can only obtain something like 75 per cent of the appraised value, this amounts to less than 50 per cent of the actual purchase price. I think that the supervisors, appraisers, assessors-whatever you want to call them-while they have been doing a commendable job have been prevented from using realistic and up to date valuations. For this reason I would urge the government to take another long, hard look at this matter.
The minister referred to what he called an economic rate, when he talked about the interest rates that are to be charged on the added amounts to the maximum limits. I am not sure where that term, economic rate,

comes from, but I think that 5 per cent is probably a maximum economic rate and, from the connotation left on that term by the minister, it seems to me he was talking about the cost to the government of the money that is going to be provided. I think that charging a rate above 5 per cent is anything but an economic rate and, if it carries very much beyond that, it will be uneconomic for farmers to purchase land.
Looking at farm costs over the past few years-and the minister has admitted this- depreciation and the other costs of maintaining machinery on farms are not only getting to be, but are now, the major cost factor. He referred to some cases where farm costs studies showed that depreciation and machinery costs amounted to over 50 per cent of the total cost of operating farms. Mr. Speaker, it would be easy to take the position that one could lay all the responsibility for this on the farm machinery companies for increasing the price of their farm equipment. But that is not quite accurate because farmers, by and large, are buying bigger equipment, more complex equipment, and therefore it follows that the price of this equipment increases. In many cases if it is used properly, and used often enough, it will pay for itself in spite of the increased cost; but nevertheless I think it is another important field that could be investigated, and we could have some action with respect to this matter of farm machinery costs.
During the last session of the legislature, the Alberta government passed a bill that in fact allows the province to underwrite the cost of certain pieces of equipment bought by a farm machinery co-operative. In my view this is another example of the provincial governments being forced to move into an area of legislation because the federal government has failed to meet its responsibilities.
There are many pieces of farm equipment which are used on a farm for but a few days each year, and it would certainly be an economic advantage for several farmers to own one of these pieces of equipment and use it for a few days in rotation. I could name a number of these pieces of equipment, but I am not going to do so because I may leave some out. In other words, I would not be able to cover the whole list.
If we accept the premise that the federal government should be primarily responsible for farm credit, then the federal government should also be prepared to accept the responsibility for providing some farm credit to small co-ops of farmers who want to buy some of this expensive machinery that could be used by more than one farm unit.
I do not want to detain the house much longer tonight because I think there are many

things in this legislation that are improvements. However, at the same time I would not like either the Minister of Agriculture or the government to think that they have solved all of the problems of farm credit in the country, simply by raising the limits and making these very few minor amendments which are proposed in Bill C-100, the bill before us tonight.
Mr. Speaker, there is also a need of land levelling with respect to large irrigation systems which have been developed over the past number of years in western Canada. One of the most desperate needs, that has not been met to date, has been for some kind of credit to be available over a long period of time so that this land can be levelled to the point where farmers can spread irrigation water economically. Once this land levelling is done, and is done properly, it enhances the value of a farm almost into perpetuity, and it never has to be done again.
It is true that at the present time there is provision under the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow money for this specific purpose, but I think we need to recognize that almost 100 per cent of the money needed for this specific purpose should be supplied through the form of credit. I say this because it enhances the value of the farmland. It immediately increases the productivity of a farm, and there is no depreciation on it at all.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, right at the present time I am having a little difficulty with the income tax department concerning some farmers who have in fact done this work, because the income tax department takes the position that there is no depreciation on farm land, that is, on this levelling; and I agree. At the same time the farmers have in fact paid out some money to do these improvements, but the income tax department will not allow them to charge it up as an operating expense because it is a capital improvement. Therefore the income tax department, or the Department of National Revenue, will have to take another look at it, and have it one way or the other. It is simply unfair for them to suggest there is no depreciation and therefore farmers cannot claim a deduction from capital cost while on the other hand suggesting it is not an operating expense.
As far as this party is concerned we are going to make one or two suggestions as we go through the clause by clause study of the bill. We think that the bill contains some improvements in the present act, but at the same time we believe that smaller borrowers should have been given consideration along the lines I suggested with respect to a different kind of appraising, and particularly by making provision in some way for those years when the farmer's income is insufficient
Farm Credit Act
to make the payments demanded of him for the year in question.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak on Bill No. C-100 amending the Farm Credit Act. I must congratulate the Minister of Agriculture for having introduced in the house this bill which involves some rather interesting amendments. We can congratulate him now to make up for the times we criticize him, because tonight he deserves it. I do not know whether it is due to the fact that his attendance in the house has been more regular that he felt more deeply the needs of the farmers, but we notice that he is getting to know his department better and that he has a fuller understanding of the subject. I want to congratulate him personally for that.
The proposed amendments will not solve all the problems besetting our farmers. But when we take action like that, we encourage our farmers to become more interested in the land.
I was listening a while ago to the minister when he said that the Farm Credit Corporation will have granted 9,875 loans in 1964. We can say that this is a progressive step when, two years ago, we find that 5,885 farm loans had been granted by the Farm Credit Corporation in 1962 and 7,438 in 1963. This year, we have 9,875 loans.
Our pace is rather normal. I believe that, with the amendments introduced this year by the minister, the year 1965 will register a new expansion of farming, in general.
Then, I see in clause 1:
The definition of "farming" is to be broadened to include bee-keeping.
That provision pleases me above anything else because, for the past three or four years, many farmers in my riding have been trying to get by as well as they could on their farms. I realize that they will welcome that amendment which will allow them to operate on a more economic basis that sector of agriculture which was forgotten by all previous governments. I understand this field of agriculture is sufficiently important to interest many beekeepers, Mr. Minister, and I am glad you thought of them.
The same thing can be said of the word "farming" in the explanatory notes. In that amendment, it seems that more emphasis is given to the real meaning of farming. I notice also in the second paragraph that the word "farmer":
-means a person whose principal occupation is farming. This amendment would enable the corporation to deem the executor or the administrator-

Farm Credit Act
How often have I seen, Mr. Minister, farms where the father had died and all the children had to leave the family home, because only the head of the family was recognized as a farmer. Now, under this amendment, the executor of the estate can administer the estate of the deceased farmer, that is to say he is considered as the farmer just like the deceased himself, no matter if the executor of the estate is the son of the deceased or a relative of the deceased. In other words, this amendment will protect and preserve many of our farms which today, after 10, 15 and 20 years, have yet to find somebody to resume farming.
Clause 2 would increase the capital of the corporation. Here again, this will permit the corporation to take another step forward. It will perhaps permit 2,000 or 3,000 more farmers to resume work on their farms, operate new farms or save old farms. In the province of Quebec, as I said earlier in the house, the question is not to take over new land at the present time, but the biggest effort is rather to get back into production abandoned land which represents a proportion of 30 or 35 per cent of all farm land.
Mr. Speaker, I was told by officials of the Farm Credit Corporation in Roberval that at the rate things are going at present, we will have granted this year from 125 to 130 loans in the Roberval constituency alone. I hope that, following the proposed amendments, we will be able to grant 200 or 250 loans next year, for even 500 loans would not be too great a number in my constituency.
Provision of clause 3 will enable a farmer to borrow from the Farm Credit Corporation to advance money to a member of his family desirous to acquire farm land. This is of great interest to farmers' sons and there are many of them in my constituency.
In fact, my constituency includes large families of farmers and the majority of the sons in those families have tried to work in industry, but since they do not have the required training, they have to come back home after five, six and even eight years of work in an industry and they try to buy land.
I have discussed this problem with the agronomist of the Roberval constituency who told me that the applications of some 40 sons of farmers who wished to buy these lands where they would have amply provided for their needs had been refused. In fact, I know these farmers; they are hard workers and the new provisions of Farm Credit Act will allow this group, which could not do so last year, to take advantage of the Farm Credit Corporation.
I am sure that, as a result of that amendment, it will be easier to help young sons of farmers who wish to return to farming.

As for the rate of interest, I hope that it will be reduced and, above all, that it will not be over 5 per cent.
The minister said a while ago that loans of $40,000 to $50,000 would be more costly. I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. I do not understand why someone who can borrow from $15,000 to $20,000, at a rate of interest of 5 per cent would have to pay more to borrow $40,000 to $50,000. No, I cannot understand that.
And if the rate of interest is set at 6 or 7 per cent in order to improve the standard of living of someone, it will certainly not be the standard of living of farmers. It will be that of the lender, of the chartered bank, or of any other lending company. If we really care to propose amendments in the interest of the farmer, let the interest rate remain at 5 per cent, while increasing the amount of loans to $40,000 and $50,000.
Mr. Speaker, I would have wished for a little more time to deal with other subjects, but a friend of mine asked me three or four minutes to make known his own point of view. I shall therefore give him the floor, but before doing so, I would like to deal with the operation of the Farm Credit Corporation. That is mainly at fault in my electoral district. But those who are dissatisfied are those who have not been able to avail themselves of such loans, because the personnel in charge of administering the act was not competent.
I already said to the house that the personnel was not competent, whether because its members were too few or because some lacked the required knowledge. There is a proverb that says: One cannot give what one does not have. If a young counsellor does not know anything, what can he do? How can he assess a land? I have found that out by myself in my own riding, and that is the reason why I asked the minister to keep his eyes open and send an investigator into the field. I am sure that this investigation will prove the truth of my allegations.
Last year I asked for an increase in the number of advisers in the province of Quebec. I am sorry the last report does not give these details, as did the report for 1962, because no comparison can be made with other provinces.
We wholeheartedly hope for an increase in that personnel and for the updating of their knowledge.

Mr. Speaker, I shall say but a few words. I do not want to miss this opportunity of discussing the bill before us.
After the speeches made by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) and

the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), I wish to point out that we should congratulate warmly the minister on the presentation of this bill. This clearly indicates-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Does the hon. member want to direct a question or to take a substantial part in the debate?
No. I wanted to take part in the debate, not in a substantial way perhaps, but in an ordinary way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. In the circumstances, I must recognize the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis).
Excuse me, Mr. Speaker. I had not seen the hon. member for Carleton. I know he is more competent than I am to speak about agriculture.

I think that the tributes which have been paid the minister in regard to this bill tonight have been quite unusual and well deserved. I was a little overwhelmed by the reference made to him by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who said he thought the minister's thinking was 40 years ahead of the thinking of his party. Certainly, in my opinion there is no question but that the philosophy of the bill is just plain, common sense and I would not embellish it with any label like socialism or anything else. It is a philosophy which will enable farmers to do a job which is today increasingly difficult for them to perform in an age in which capital is more and more important.
There is no question but that this act, which is under the administration of the Department of Agriculture, is the proper machinery for the extension of farm credit. I am very happy with the amendments which are coming forward and which will mean, in effect, that instead of the industrial development bank getting increasingly into this area, as it has been as a result of vertical integration, the administration will be in the hands of the department whose orientation is more in the direction of service than it is in the direction of straight financial administration. I believe the hon. member for Kootenay West made this point and made it very well in the course of his speech.
The transfer of the administration of the Farm Credit Corporation from the Department of Finance to the Department of Agriculture does represent a fundamental change in the philosophy of that act, and the amendments which are coming forward are in keeping with that spirit.
I presume it is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

PRAIRIE PROVINCES
subsubtopic: CLOSING OF RAILWAY STATIONS AND REMOVAL OF AGENTS
speechtext:
The question I wish to debate tonight is a simple one. Although Mr. Speaker ruled the other afternoon, it should be put on the order paper, he did not state why it should be put on the order paper rather than answered in the house. I suggest it is an urgent question and it is one which is directly related to rail line abandonment.
At the present time there is on the prairies, as hon. members know, an agreement between the railway companies and the government that no action will be taken to proceed with rail line abandonment until a complete survey of the situation has been made. I understand that such a survey is under way at the present time. My question to the government was this: Will the government consider freezing the action of the railway companies at the present time in making application to the board of transport commissioners to close certain branch line stations and do away with station agents? Steps of this sort are very similar to abandoning the line itself. As there

-I would ask the parliamentary secretary, then, to request the minister to give this matter his serious consideration. As I have just said, this action by the railway companies is tantamount to rail line abandonment. I have had experience of these applications by the railways and it is my personal opinion that the companies know what conditions should exist before the board of transport commissioners will entertain applications for abandonment. In my opinion the railway companies do everything within their power to see that these conditions exist before they make applications. In one case I have in mind they even took the telephone out of a station so that the people in the area could not telephone to the station agent to find out when a train was due to arrive. I might say that on branch lines trains seldom run to schedule. People would not know when perishable goods were coming in. Moreover, there are no modern facilities in many of these stations. They are of old vintage. Some of the old prairie towns have been modernizing themselves in latter years, but the railway companies do nothing at all to introduce people to patronize their

mode of transportation. In other words, it would appear to me, as one who comes from the prairies, that the railway companies are only concerned with making money out of handling grain; they are not concerned with the service they can give the people on the prairies.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary if as soon as possible he would request the board of transport commissioners or the minister to give early consideration to preventing the consideration of these applications until the survey has been completed. I do not wish to say more at the present time. I hope the hon. gentleman has got my point. It is one which is directly related to rail line abandonment and it amounts to practically the same thing, particularly in areas where permission is given by the board of transport commissioners.
